title: Secrets management
summary: Where passwords, API keys, tokens and certificates are kept, how applications get them, and what happens when one leaks.
scope: Every secret used by a company application, pipeline or script. Personal passwords of employees are covered by the password policy instead.

resources.title: Secret Manager how-to
resources.description: How to add a secret and read it from Go, Java, Node and Python.

requirements.title: Secrets live in Secret Manager
requirements.statement: Every secret an application or pipeline uses is stored in Secret Manager and read from there at run time.
requirements.rationale: One place means one place to rotate, to restrict and to audit. Secrets copied into files and variables are forgotten and never rotated.
guidance: Add the secret to Secret Manager in the project of the application.
Give read access only to the service account of the application.
Read the secret at start-up through the platform library, not from a file in the image.

verification.description: Code review and the yearly security audit.

lookFor: A password, key or token read from an environment variable that is set in a deployment file
A secret value in a Kubernetes manifest, Helm values file or Terraform variable

requirements.title: No secrets in source code
requirements.statement: No secret is written in source code, configuration files, test data or documentation that is committed to Git, not even for test environments.
requirements.rationale: Git keeps everything forever and repositories are copied to many laptops. A committed secret has to be treated as leaked.
guidance: Use a placeholder such as ${DB_PASSWORD} and read the value from Secret Manager.
For tests, generate a throw-away secret when the test starts.

verification.description: Secret scanner on every pull request; a finding blocks the merge.

lookFor: String literals that look like keys, tokens or passwords
Files named .env, credentials.json or *.pem added to the repository
A test that uses a real-looking secret instead of a generated one

requirements.title: Rotate a leaked secret at once
requirements.statement: A secret that was exposed is replaced and the old value revoked within 24 hours, and Cyber Security is told straight away.
requirements.rationale: Attackers scan public repositories and chat exports for keys within minutes.
guidance: Follow the process 'Rotate a leaked secret'.
Do not wait to find out whether the secret was used before rotating it.

verification.description: Checked by Cyber Security for every reported leak.

requirements.title: Rotate production secrets every year
requirements.statement: Secrets used in production are replaced at least every 12 months, or every 90 days when they give access to personal data.
requirements.rationale: Regular rotation limits how long a secret that leaked unnoticed stays useful.
guidance: Turn on automatic rotation in Secret Manager where the provider supports it.
Otherwise set a rotation reminder on the secret.

verification.description: A weekly report lists production secrets older than their rotation period.

requirements.title: Use workload identity instead of cloud keys
requirements.statement: Applications and pipelines reach Google Cloud and Azure with workload identity, not with downloaded service account keys.
requirements.rationale: A key file can be copied and used from anywhere; workload identity only works from the workload itself.
guidance: Bind the Kubernetes service account to the cloud service account.
In GitHub Actions, use the shared workflow's identity step instead of a key secret.

lookFor: GOOGLE_APPLICATION_CREDENTIALS pointing at a key file
A step that writes a service account key from a secret to disk

requirements.title: Read secrets through the platform library
requirements.statement: Services read secrets with the platform library of their language, which caches them and picks up a new version without a restart.
requirements.rationale: Hand-written secret loading often logs the value on error or never refreshes it.

lookFor: Direct calls to the Secret Manager client in application code
Secrets read once into a global variable at start-up

requirements.title: Secret scan before each commit
requirements.statement: Developers may run the secret scanner as a pre-commit hook so that a secret never leaves their laptop.
requirements.rationale: The pipeline finds a secret after it was pushed, when it already counts as leaked.
guidance: Run 'make install-hooks' from the security-tools repository once.
